Imputes detailed income components to create “synthetic taxpayers” with higher incomes than typically captured in the FRS. These records initially have zero weight but can be upweighted during calibration to match HMRC income distribution targets.
Advani-Summers capital gains distribution data; HMRC Capital Gains Tax statistics, Table 2.1a (individuals, by size of gain)

Not a QRF. Advani and Summers give, for each band of total income, the share of people with gains and the percentiles of those gains. HMRC gives the number of individuals with a CGT liability, and their gains, by size of gain. The imputation takes who holds gains from the first and how many hold how much from the second.
Each household’s first adult draws a gain from their income band’s Advani-Summers distribution.

Where the draw is above the lowest HMRC size band limit (the £3,000 annual exempt amount), the household is stacked again as a has-gains twin carrying the gain. The split propensity adjusts Advani-Summers’ share of all people in the income band for assignment to first adults only. This is the propensity before rejecting draws of £3,000 or less; rejecting those draws lowers realised incidence. For a zero-weight (SPI synthetic) household, complementary original and twin calibration priors are carried into calibration. The prior-equivalent weight sets only the twin’s household weight, while the original’s household weight remains zero. Smaller draws, including losses, get no twin: HMRC publishes liable taxpayers only, so nothing would anchor them.

The spline stops at each band’s 95th percentile, so few draws exceed £500,000 and none exceeds about £2m. For each HMRC size band from £500,000 up, 30 donor households are stacked carrying the band’s published mean gain.

Calibration targets the taxpayer count and the gains of each HMRC size band, and their totals. Before the first epoch it scales the starting weights so that each band’s taxpayer count is on its target.

Census private-rented households by BRMA and bedrooms (not QRF; applied when the base FRS dataset is built)
The FRS identifies only the region, but Local Housing Allowance rates vary by Broad Rental Market Area (BRMA).
draws each benefit unit’s BRMA within its region, in proportion to the private-rented households in each BRMA:
shared-accommodation and one-bedroom LHA categories use one-bedroom homes;
the two-, three- and four-or-more-bedroom categories use homes with that many bedrooms;
Northern Ireland’s census has no bedrooms, so its weights are the same for every category.
